The book swap messages

The library has a book swap. People can choose used books there. The swap is on Saturday 17 October. Here are four records about it.

N. The library notice
Lena Vale works at the library. On Monday 12 October, Lena wrote this note to help people plan a visit:
“Book swap: Garden Room. Saturday, 10 am to noon. Entry is free. You do not need to bring a book.”

R. The room sheet
Ari Chen books the rooms. On Friday 16 October, Ari wrote this room sheet:
“Garden Room: being painted.
Book swap: moved to Cedar Room. Saturday, 10 am to noon.”
Ari signed the sheet. It tells staff where to set up the books.

P. Jo's post
Jo Reed helps at a bookmark stall. On Friday, Jo wrote:
“Come to the book swap in the Cedar Room! It runs from 10 am to noon. Entry costs $2. Come to our stall, too!”
Jo copied the room and time from Ari's sheet. Jo wants people to visit the stall. Money from the stall buys more library books.

S. The stall card
Nia Shah runs the stall. On Friday, Nia made a card to explain the cost:
“A handmade bookmark costs $2. You can choose to buy one. Entry to the swap is free. You can come without a book.”

These are the records the class has on Friday. The class is making a short note for Saturday's visitors.

Planning for the book swap

Riverside Library is holding a book swap on Saturday 17 October. Visitors will be able to choose used books, and they do not have to bring one. The class is preparing a visitor note using four records collected on Friday.

N. A notice for visitors
Librarian Lena Vale wrote a notice on Monday 12 October to help people arrange a visit. It said: “Book swap, Garden Room, Saturday from 10 am until noon. Entry is free.” The library put Lena's name at the bottom, and a copy was still on the noticeboard on Friday.

R. A record for staff
The room-booking sheet was updated on Friday 16 October. Bookings officer Ari Chen signed it after changing the rooms. Its entries said: “Garden Room: being painted. Book swap: moved to Cedar Room, Saturday 10 am–noon.” Staff use this sheet when they set up an event. The Monday notice was still beside it on the board.

P. A post for the community
Jo Reed volunteers at the bookmark stall. On Friday, Jo posted: “Come to the book swap in the Cedar Room, 10 am–noon. Entry costs $2. Visit our handmade-bookmark stall while you are there!” Jo added a source note: “Room and time copied from Ari's Friday booking sheet.” Jo wanted more visitors at the stall because its sales would pay for new library books.

S. A card for customers
Stall organiser Nia Shah prepared the Friday stall card. It read: “Handmade bookmarks: $2 each. Buying one is optional. Book swap entry is free, and you may come without bringing a book.” Nia made the card so customers could tell what they were paying for. In this card, optional means that visitors can choose whether to buy.

The class has the notice, the booking sheet, Jo's post and Nia's card. Before its visitor note goes out, the class needs to decide which room and cost details the records support.

One event, four records

A class at Riverside Library is preparing a short guide to Saturday's book swap, where visitors can choose used books without bringing a book of their own. The event is on 17 October. By Friday afternoon, the class has collected four records, but the details do not all agree.

N. From the library noticeboard
“Book swap: Saturday, 10 am–noon, Garden Room. Free entry.” Beneath those details, librarian Lena Vale has signed and dated the notice Monday 12 October. Its heading, “Plan your library visit”, explains its job. A copy remains on the board on Friday, although the room-booking sheet beside it bears a later date.

R. From the room-booking sheet
Bookings officer Ari Chen's signed Friday 16 October record lists the Garden Room as “being painted”. The next entry reads: “Book swap moved to Cedar Room; Saturday, 10 am–noon.” These entries tell staff where to prepare each event. There is no entry charge listed on this sheet; its columns are for rooms, activities and times.

P. From the community feed
“Come along to the Cedar Room this Saturday! The book swap runs from 10 am until noon. Entry costs $2, and our handmade-bookmark stall will be there.” Jo Reed, a stall volunteer, posted the message on Friday. Readers can follow its source note: “Room and time copied from Ari's Friday booking sheet.” The note names no source for the entry charge.

S. From the stall record
On Friday, stall organiser Nia Shah prepared this wording for the sales desk: “Handmade bookmarks: $2 each. Purchase is optional. Book swap entry is free; no book is needed to attend.” A short note tells volunteers to display the wording so visitors understand exactly what a payment buys.

Why the stall is being promoted
Jo has also written, below the community post, “I want more people to visit our stall. Every bookmark we sell helps us buy new books for the library.” The class includes this line in its source folder rather than putting it into the guide as an event rule.

The guide has space for the room, the time and a sentence about cost. The class has Friday's records, not a report from Saturday's event. Its editor wants each detail supported, with any uncertainty left visible.

Preparing a visitor brief

Before Riverside Library's Saturday 17 October book swap, a class is assembling a visitor brief. People may choose used books without donating any; the practical details, however, have reached the class through records produced for different audiences. The folder closes on Friday afternoon, before the event takes place.

N. Notice retained on the board
Issued on Monday 12 October and signed by librarian Lena Vale, the notice reads: “Plan your visit: book swap, Garden Room, Saturday, 10 am–noon. Entry free.” The library's name appears above it. A Friday photograph of the board shows the notice still displayed beside a more recent room sheet. Nothing in the photograph establishes when either document was last checked.

R. Staff booking record
Ari Chen, the bookings officer, signed the revised sheet on Friday 16 October. Two consecutive entries record “Garden Room: being painted” and “Book swap moved to Cedar Room, Saturday 10 am–noon”. Its purpose is to direct staff preparing rooms. The sheet has columns for room, activity and time, but none for admission charges.

P. Community post
“Cedar Room, 10 am–noon this Saturday: come to the book swap! Entry $2. Our handmade-bookmark stall will be there, too.” The Friday post is attributed to Jo Reed, a stall volunteer. A source line credits Ari's Friday sheet for “room and time”; it makes no corresponding attribution for the fee. Jo describes the purpose below the post: “I want more visitors at the stall because every sale helps buy new library books.”

S. Sales-desk wording
Nia Shah, the stall organiser, approved a card on Friday: “Handmade bookmarks, $2 each; purchase optional. Book swap entry free. Visitors need not bring a book.” The accompanying instruction asks volunteers to display the card where customers can distinguish payment for an item from entry to the event. There is no record showing that Jo saw this card before posting.

Editorial choices
The class's draft brief has three blank fields: room, time and cost. One editor proposes using the library notice throughout because its author works there. Another proposes taking every detail from the Friday post because it is newer. Neither proposal accounts for every record in the folder. The brief will identify its information as current to Friday rather than report that Saturday's arrangements have already been observed.

The four documents remain available beside the draft. Their dates, stated purposes and attributed sources will have to do more work than a general label such as “official” or “community”.

A visitor brief and its evidential limits

The class compiling Riverside Library's visitor brief has a modest commission: give families usable information about the book swap on Saturday 17 October, when they may choose used books without contributing any of their own. Its source folder, closed on Friday afternoon, contains neither an account of the event itself nor an undertaking that the arrangements cannot change. What it does contain is a small disagreement whose apparent simplicity has divided the editors.

N. The public notice
“Plan your visit: book swap, Garden Room, Saturday, 10 am–noon. Entry free.” Issued on Monday 12 October under librarian Lena Vale's name, the notice remains on the library board in a photograph taken on Friday. Its institutional heading and named author make its origin traceable; the photograph establishes continued display, but records no renewed check of the wording. The notice was designed to help visitors arrange their day, not to document subsequent changes to room allocations.

R. The operational record
On Friday 16 October, bookings officer Ari Chen signed a revision to the staff sheet: “Garden Room: being painted”; immediately below it, “Book swap moved to Cedar Room, Saturday 10 am–noon”. The columns record rooms, activities and times. They contain no field for admission charges. Intended to guide staff setting up events, this document is narrower in purpose than the public notice, although the two now compete for a reader's attention on the same board.

P. The circulating message
Jo Reed, a volunteer at the handmade-bookmark stall, posted on Friday: “Cedar Room, 10 am–noon this Saturday! Come to the book swap. Entry $2. Visit our stall while you are there.” A source line reads, precisely, “Room and time copied from Ari's Friday booking sheet.” No equivalent attribution accompanies the charge. Below the post is a separate explanation: “I want more people to visit the stall; every bookmark we sell pays towards new library books.”

The class's source folder includes a screenshot of Jo's post shared by a second community account. That account has added no observations, checked details or named sources; the wording, including the source line, is unchanged. In the margin, one editor writes, “Two appearances: twice the support for both details.” Another has drawn a line back to Jo's original source note but left no comment.

S. The sales-desk record
Stall organiser Nia Shah's Friday card specifies “Handmade bookmarks: $2 each. Purchase optional. Book swap entry free; no book required.” Its accompanying instruction is to display the card where customers can see what a payment buys. The folder does not establish whether Jo had seen this card, whether the post's charge resulted from a misunderstanding, or whether any later correction was made. Nia's record and Lena's earlier notice agree about free entry, whereas only the former explains the $2 transaction.

The proposed brief
One draft would reproduce the library notice, treating its named institutional authorship as sufficient for all three practical details. A second would use the newer post throughout, counting its repeated appearance in the community feed as further support. The disagreement is therefore not merely over which room to print: each draft adopts a rule that carries an unstated claim about the relationship between origin, currency and corroboration.

The final brief has room for a location, a time, a concise cost statement and a source-date note. Its readers need usable guidance, but the editors' access to the records does not give them access to the authors' private intentions or to Saturday's future events. Their wording must work within that distinction.

Alpha.text:
The book swap messages

The library has a book swap. People can choose used books there. The swap is on Saturday 17 October. Here are four records about it.

N. The library notice
Lena Vale works at the library. On Monday 12 October, Lena wrote this note to help people plan a visit:
“Book swap: Garden Room. Saturday, 10 am to noon. Entry is free. You do not need to bring a book.”

R. The room sheet
Ari Chen books the rooms. On Friday 16 October, Ari wrote this room sheet:
“Garden Room: being painted.
Book swap: moved to Cedar Room. Saturday, 10 am to noon.”
Ari signed the sheet. It tells staff where to set up the books.

P. Jo's post
Jo Reed helps at a bookmark stall. On Friday, Jo wrote:
“Come to the book swap in the Cedar Room! It runs from 10 am to noon. Entry costs $2. Come to our stall, too!”
Jo copied the room and time from Ari's sheet. Jo wants people to visit the stall. Money from the stall buys more library books.

S. The stall card
Nia Shah runs the stall. On Friday, Nia made a card to explain the cost:
“A handmade bookmark costs $2. You can choose to buy one. Entry to the swap is free. You can come without a book.”

These are the records the class has on Friday. The class is making a short note for Saturday's visitors.

Beta.text:
Planning for the book swap

Riverside Library is holding a book swap on Saturday 17 October. Visitors will be able to choose used books, and they do not have to bring one. The class is preparing a visitor note using four records collected on Friday.

N. A notice for visitors
Librarian Lena Vale wrote a notice on Monday 12 October to help people arrange a visit. It said: “Book swap, Garden Room, Saturday from 10 am until noon. Entry is free.” The library put Lena's name at the bottom, and a copy was still on the noticeboard on Friday.

R. A record for staff
The room-booking sheet was updated on Friday 16 October. Bookings officer Ari Chen signed it after changing the rooms. Its entries said: “Garden Room: being painted. Book swap: moved to Cedar Room, Saturday 10 am–noon.” Staff use this sheet when they set up an event. The Monday notice was still beside it on the board.

P. A post for the community
Jo Reed volunteers at the bookmark stall. On Friday, Jo posted: “Come to the book swap in the Cedar Room, 10 am–noon. Entry costs $2. Visit our handmade-bookmark stall while you are there!” Jo added a source note: “Room and time copied from Ari's Friday booking sheet.” Jo wanted more visitors at the stall because its sales would pay for new library books.

S. A card for customers
Stall organiser Nia Shah prepared the Friday stall card. It read: “Handmade bookmarks: $2 each. Buying one is optional. Book swap entry is free, and you may come without bringing a book.” Nia made the card so customers could tell what they were paying for. In this card, optional means that visitors can choose whether to buy.

The class has the notice, the booking sheet, Jo's post and Nia's card. Before its visitor note goes out, the class needs to decide which room and cost details the records support.

Gamma.text:
One event, four records

A class at Riverside Library is preparing a short guide to Saturday's book swap, where visitors can choose used books without bringing a book of their own. The event is on 17 October. By Friday afternoon, the class has collected four records, but the details do not all agree.

N. From the library noticeboard
“Book swap: Saturday, 10 am–noon, Garden Room. Free entry.” Beneath those details, librarian Lena Vale has signed and dated the notice Monday 12 October. Its heading, “Plan your library visit”, explains its job. A copy remains on the board on Friday, although the room-booking sheet beside it bears a later date.

R. From the room-booking sheet
Bookings officer Ari Chen's signed Friday 16 October record lists the Garden Room as “being painted”. The next entry reads: “Book swap moved to Cedar Room; Saturday, 10 am–noon.” These entries tell staff where to prepare each event. There is no entry charge listed on this sheet; its columns are for rooms, activities and times.

P. From the community feed
“Come along to the Cedar Room this Saturday! The book swap runs from 10 am until noon. Entry costs $2, and our handmade-bookmark stall will be there.” Jo Reed, a stall volunteer, posted the message on Friday. Readers can follow its source note: “Room and time copied from Ari's Friday booking sheet.” The note names no source for the entry charge.

S. From the stall record
On Friday, stall organiser Nia Shah prepared this wording for the sales desk: “Handmade bookmarks: $2 each. Purchase is optional. Book swap entry is free; no book is needed to attend.” A short note tells volunteers to display the wording so visitors understand exactly what a payment buys.

Epsilon.text:
A visitor brief and its evidential limits

The class compiling Riverside Library's visitor brief has a modest commission: give families usable information about the book swap on Saturday 17 October, when they may choose used books without contributing any of their own. Its source folder, closed on Friday afternoon, contains neither an account of the event itself nor an undertaking that the arrangements cannot change. What it does contain is a small disagreement whose apparent simplicity has divided the editors.

N. The public notice
“Plan your visit: book swap, Garden Room, Saturday, 10 am–noon. Entry free.” Issued on Monday 12 October under librarian Lena Vale's name, the notice remains on the library board in a photograph taken on Friday. Its institutional heading and named author make its origin traceable; the photograph establishes continued display, but records no renewed check of the wording. The notice was designed to help visitors arrange their day, not to document subsequent changes to room allocations.

R. The operational record
On Friday 16 October, bookings officer Ari Chen signed a revision to the staff sheet: “Garden Room: being painted”; immediately below it, “Book swap moved to Cedar Room, Saturday 10 am–noon”. The columns record rooms, activities and times. They contain no field for admission charges. Intended to guide staff setting up events, this document is narrower in purpose than the public notice, although the two now compete for a reader's attention on the same board.

P. The circulating message
Jo Reed, a volunteer at the handmade-bookmark stall, posted on Friday: “Cedar Room, 10 am–noon this Saturday! Come to the book swap. Entry $2. Visit our stall while you are there.” A source line reads, precisely, “Room and time copied from Ari's Friday booking sheet.” No equivalent attribution accompanies the charge. Below the post is a separate explanation: “I want more people to visit the stall; every bookmark we sell pays towards new library books.”

The class's source folder includes a screenshot of Jo's post shared by a second community account. That account has added no observations, checked details or named sources; the wording, including the source line, is unchanged. In the margin, one editor writes, “Two appearances: twice the support for both details.” Another has drawn a line back to Jo's original source note but left no comment.

S. The sales-desk record
Stall organiser Nia Shah's Friday card specifies “Handmade bookmarks: $2 each. Purchase optional. Book swap entry free; no book required.” Its accompanying instruction is to display the card where customers can see what a payment buys. The folder does not establish whether Jo had seen this card, whether the post's charge resulted from a misunderstanding, or whether any later correction was made. Nia's record and Lena's earlier notice agree about free entry, whereas only the former explains the $2 transaction.

The proposed brief
One draft would reproduce the library notice, treating its named institutional authorship as sufficient for all three practical details. A second would use the newer post throughout, counting its repeated appearance in the community feed as further support. The disagreement is therefore not merely over which room to print: each draft adopts a rule that carries an unstated claim about the relationship between origin, currency and corroboration.

The final brief has room for a location, a time, a concise cost statement and a source-date note. Its readers need usable guidance, but the editors' access to the records does not give them access to the authors' private intentions or to Saturday's future events. Their wording must work within that distinction.

Preparing a visitor brief

Before Riverside Library's Saturday 17 October book swap, a class is assembling a visitor brief. People may choose used books without donating any; the practical details, however, have reached the class through records produced for different audiences. The folder closes on Friday afternoon, before the event takes place.

N. Notice retained on the board
Issued on Monday 12 October and signed by librarian Lena Vale, the notice reads: “Plan your visit: book swap, Garden Room, Saturday, 10 am–noon. Entry free.” The library's name appears above it. A Friday photograph of the board shows the notice still displayed beside a more recent room sheet. Nothing in the photograph establishes when either document was last checked.

R. Staff booking record
Ari Chen, the bookings officer, signed the revised sheet on Friday 16 October. Two consecutive entries record “Garden Room: being painted” and “Book swap moved to Cedar Room, Saturday 10 am–noon”. Its purpose is to direct staff preparing rooms. The sheet has columns for room, activity and time, but none for admission charges.

P. Community post
“Cedar Room, 10 am–noon this Saturday: come to the book swap! Entry $2. Our handmade-bookmark stall will be there, too.” The Friday post is attributed to Jo Reed, a stall volunteer. A source line credits Ari's Friday sheet for “room and time”; it makes no corresponding attribution for the fee. Jo describes the purpose below the post: “I want more visitors at the stall because every sale helps buy new library books.”

S. Sales-desk wording
Nia Shah, the stall organiser, approved a card on Friday: “Handmade bookmarks, $2 each; purchase optional. Book swap entry free. Visitors need not bring a book.” The accompanying instruction asks volunteers to display the card where customers can distinguish payment for an item from entry to the event. There is no record showing that Jo saw this card before posting.

Editorial choices
The class's draft brief has three blank fields: room, time and cost. One editor proposes using the library notice throughout because its author works there. Another proposes taking every detail from the Friday post because it is newer. Neither proposal accounts for every record in the folder. The brief will identify its information as current to Friday rather than report that Saturday's arrangements have already been observed.

The four documents remain available beside the draft. Their dates, stated purposes and attributed sources will have to do more work than a general label such as “official” or “community”.

Epsilon.text:
A visitor brief and its evidential limits

The class compiling Riverside Library's visitor brief has a modest commission: give families usable information about the book swap on Saturday 17 October, when they may choose used books without contributing any of their own. Its source folder, closed on Friday afternoon, contains neither an account of the event itself nor an undertaking that the arrangements cannot change. What it does contain is a small disagreement whose apparent simplicity has divided the editors.

N. The public notice
“Plan your visit: book swap, Garden Room, Saturday, 10 am–noon. Entry free.” Issued on Monday 12 October under librarian Lena Vale's name, the notice remains on the library board in a photograph taken on Friday. Its institutional heading and named author make its origin traceable; the photograph establishes continued display, but records no renewed check of the wording. The notice was designed to help visitors arrange their day, not to document subsequent changes to room allocations.

R. The operational record
On Friday 16 October, bookings officer Ari Chen signed a revision to the staff sheet: “Garden Room: being painted”; immediately below it, “Book swap moved to Cedar Room, Saturday 10 am–noon”. The columns record rooms, activities and times. They contain no field for admission charges. Intended to guide staff setting up events, this document is narrower in purpose than the public notice, although the two now compete for a reader's attention on the same board.

P. The circulating message
Jo Reed, a volunteer at the handmade-bookmark stall, posted on Friday: “Cedar Room, 10 am–noon this Saturday! Come to the book swap. Entry $2. Visit our stall while you are there.” A source line reads, precisely, “Room and time copied from Ari's Friday booking sheet.” No equivalent attribution accompanies the charge. Below the post is a separate explanation: “I want more people to visit the stall; every bookmark we sell pays towards new library books.”

The class's source folder includes a screenshot of Jo's post shared by a second community account. That account has added no observations, checked details or named sources; the wording, including the source line, is unchanged. In the margin, one editor writes, “Two appearances: twice the support for both details.” Another has drawn a line back to Jo's original source note but left no comment.

S. The sales-desk record
Stall organiser Nia Shah's Friday card specifies “Handmade bookmarks: $2 each. Purchase optional. Book swap entry free; no book required.” Its accompanying instruction is to display the card where customers can see what a payment buys. The folder does not establish whether Jo had seen this card, whether the post's charge resulted from a misunderstanding, or whether any later correction was made. Nia's record and Lena's earlier notice agree about free entry, whereas only the former explains the $2 transaction.

The proposed brief
One draft would reproduce the library notice, treating its named institutional authorship as sufficient for all three practical details. A second would use the newer post throughout, counting its repeated appearance in the community feed as further support. The disagreement is therefore not merely over which room to print: each draft adopts a rule that carries an unstated claim about the relationship between origin, currency and corroboration.

The final brief has room for a location, a time, a concise cost statement and a source-date note. Its readers need usable guidance, but the editors' access to the records does not give them access to the authors' private intentions or to Saturday's future events. Their wording must work within that distinction.
